sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

Introduction Scaling Transformer [1] language models involves deciding both how much parameter capacity to allocate and how to organize it [2, 3]. Depth and width are two conventional architectural choices: stacking more blocks in sequence or enlarging the transformations within each block [46]. Recent advances in LLM architectures have substantially expanded the design space within this template through innovations in attention mechanisms [7, 8], sparse expert computation [9], and residual connections [1012], while the sequential composition of full blocks remains common foundation. In this work, we explore branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks, as complementary way to organize and scale model parameters, and ask: Can Transformers scale more effectively and efficiently through parallel compositions of full blocks? To this end, we introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which enables parallel computation at the granularity of full Transformer blocks (Figure 1(a)). An MBT processes the input through shared initial layers (the prelude1) , splits computation across 𝐾 independently parameterized branches that execute concurrently, fuses their outputs, and passes the result through shared final layers (the coda). The key idea is to preserve sequential composition within each branch while allowing subsequent shared layers to build on the results of multiple transformation paths. In comparison, related work on parallel Transformer architectures explores different design axes (Figure 2): concurrency within individual blocks [14], allocation of width and depth [46], or alternative parallel computation paths [15]. Systems approaches such as tensor and pipeline parallelism [16] are orthogonal to and compatible with this architectural design. Relative to standard Transformer, an MBT can be defined in three ways at comparable compute: Wide-Shallow MBTs preserve the baselines block width and distribute its blocks across branches; Narrow-Deep MBTs preserve the baselines depth along each branch using narrower blocks; and Balanced MBTs interpolate between these choices by jointly adjusting branch width and depth. To further exploit the parallel branch structure of MBTs, we propose Joint-KV, which constructs shared key-value (KV) cache from all branch representations at each depth while retaining separate queries for each branch (Figure 4). For 𝐾 branches, this reduces cache storage in the branch region to 1 𝐾 of Independent-KV at fixed branch depth and KV dimensions. We combine Joint-KV with Balanced MBTs as our final model recipes (Figure 1(b)). To translate our architectural design into practical inference gains, we develop an inference engine based on nano-vLLM [17, 18] that exploits the parallel branches and shared KV caches through branch grouping and head folding, reducing sequential execution steps and redundant KV reads during decoding. / Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and efficiency of MBT. First, branching improves language modeling performance. Across scaling ladder of mixture-of-experts models (0.8B-2.1B total parameters), our scaling laws first indicate that the best 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBT matches standard Transformer trained with 1.23 as much compute, while allocating approximately 79% of blocks to parallel branches yields performance on par with the standard Transformer. Balanced MBTs achieve the strongest performance among the studied allocations and maintain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. Second, Joint-KV MBTs, together with our inference engine, substantially improve inference speed while retaining strong modeling performance. In particular, 2-, 3-, and 4-branch Joint-KV MBTs match standard Transformers trained with 1.161.26 as much training body compute, while reducing KV cache size by 1934%. On single H200 GPU, our models achieve up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput than the standard Transformer with 64K-token inputs and 8 concurrent requests. Extensive ablation studies spanning five scaling sweeps further demonstrate that the benefits of branching extend beyond conventional adjustments to model width and depth. Sharing KV caches reduces storage, but separate attention calls for different branches can still reload the same KV data. Head folding folds the branch dimension into the query-head dimension, grouping queries by their shared KV head so that all branches use single grouped-query attention (GQA) call [20]. This allows the attention kernel to reuse shared KV data across branches, reducing redundant memory traffic. Each query head still computes its own softmax over the same keys and values, preserving the attention function itself. Distributed Execution. MBTs can be distributed through tensor parallelism or branch parallelism. With Joint-KV, these layouts differ in shared KV-cache construction. With tensor parallelism, devices replicate branch hidden states while sharding projection weights and attention heads. Each device constructs its assigned shared KV heads locally, without an additional collective. Head folding also remains local when the corresponding query heads from all branches are placed on the same device. Alternatively, branches can run on different devices. Each device computes its branchs contribution to the shared KV projection, and an all-reduce combines these contributions before attention at each depth. The all-reduce operates on tensor of width 2ℎKV𝑑ℎ, avoiding an all-gather of branch representations of total width 𝐾 𝑑𝑏. At fixed KV dimensions, its per-token tensor size is independent of the branch count, although communication cost depends on the group size and topology. This layout distributes branch weights and computation across devices but requires synchronization at every branch depth. This layout may be useful when branch sharding is needed to fit the model in memory and fast interconnects are available. 3. Experiments

sections.title: 4.1 Width and Depth Ablations
sections.content: Ablation Goal. We test whether the gains of branching can be explained by shallower, wider network, and whether they persist when Standards depth is preserved. Setup. We retain Standard and 2-branch WideShallow MBT as fixed references at each scale, with roughly half the blocks in parallel branches in the latter. We add three controls. Global wideshallow widens the entire sequential stack and matches WideShallow MBTs depth, following the conventional widthdepth trade-off [6]. Local wide-core is our localized control: it replaces the two branches with one wider core of the same depth, preserving the prelude and coda. Both controls test whether fewer, wider sequential blocks can recover the gains of WideShallow MBT at comparable compute. NarrowDeep MBT instead keeps the same prelude and coda, together roughly half of Standards blocks, and gives each of two narrower branches the full depth of Standards middle stack. It thus serves as depth-matched ablation against Standard models. Table 4 gives W1 example. Full configurations appear in Table 13. Result and Interpretation. Figure 10 shows that WideShallow MBT outperforms both widening baselines (Global WideShallow and Local WideCore) at all four scales, with consistently better-fitted scaling curve. NarrowDeep MBT also outperforms Standard across all scales and exhibits the steepest scaling exponent (𝛼 = 0.0548, versus 0.0515 for WideShallow), suggesting that branching improves modeling quality even when the original sequential depth is preserved. Together, these results demonstrate benefits beyond sequential widening at matched depth, while indicating that the best MBT can be tuned by jointly considering width and depth. 11 Multi-Branch Transformer Table 4. sections.content: Ablation Goal. At the same KV-cache size and training budget, does constructing shared keys and values jointly across branches (Joint-KV) improve modeling quality over keeping smaller, independent caches in each branch? On the main ladder, the shared KV heads cannot always be split evenly between two branches (e.g., W2 and W4), so an exactly cache-matched Independent-KV control does not exist at every scale. sections.title: 4.4 Branch Placement
sections.content: Ablation Goal and Setup. We test where to branch by placing the parallel blocks in the early, middle (ours), or late layers. We use 2-branch WideShallow MBT at scale W3, with 16 blocks in total, 8 of which are distributed across the parallel branches. Result and Interpretation. As shown in Figure 11, middle placement achieves the lowest loss (2.445), outperforming both early (2.458) and late (2.464) branching. The advantage of early over late branching suggests that retaining shared coda is more beneficial than retaining shared prelude in this setting. Overall, these results favor placing the parallel region in the middle layers. 5. Related Work Parallelism in large language models. Architectural work on language models explores concurrency within individual blocks, as in PaLM [14], widthdepth trade-offs in sequential stacks [46], and parallel passes through shared backbone with learned prefixes, as in ParScale [15]. From systems perspective, parallelism supports efficient execution across devices: tensor and pipeline parallelism distribute model computation [16], and track 13 Multi-Branch Transformer Figure 11. Branching in the middle works best. At W3, we place 8 shared blocks around two 4-block branches while holding all other settings fixed. Shared processing before and after the branches gives the lowest loss. parallelism uses narrower stacks with periodic synchronization to reduce communication overhead [37]. Our approach explores an architectural design axis orthogonal to those studied in prior work on parallel language models, while remaining compatible with existing systems approaches. More broadly, multi-branch architectures have long history in computer vision, with prominent examples including Inception [38], ResNeXt [39], FractalNet [40], and HRNet [41]. Earlier NLP work (Pre-LLM era) explored parallel branches within attention modules [42, 43] and encoder backbones [44]. However, parallel composition of full Transformer blocks remains underexplored as means of scaling modern autoregressive language models. Information flow and KV-cache sharing. Recent work improves information flow through expanded residual streams and selective aggregation of representations across depth [1012, 45, 46]. These approaches enrich interactions within sequential block stack, although maintaining and mixing additional representations can introduce extra memory traffic. MBT takes different approach by reorganizing full Transformer blocks into parallel branches and fusing their outputs before subsequent shared layers. Prior work shares keys and values across attention heads [20, 47] or across decoder layers, as in Cross-Layer Attention and YOCO [48, 49]. Joint-KV shares along different axis that exists only in multi-branch models: across parallel branches at the same depth, while retaining branch-specific queries. This axis is orthogonal to head and layer sharing (our models already combine it with GQA) and enables head folding to reduce redundant KV reads during long-context decoding. Our results show that the resulting cache savings and inference gains coexist with stronger language modeling performance than standard Transformers. 6. Conclusion We introduced MBTs, which organize full Transformer blocks into parallel branches between shared initial and final layers. Across four MoE model scales, branching improves language-model quality and fitted scaling at comparable training compute. Balanced branch allocations, Joint-KV, and an inference engine that exploits branch structure together enable better modeling quality and faster decoding. These results establish branching as practical architectural choice alongside width and depth. These findings open several directions for future work: Joint Scaling Laws with Branching. Existing scaling studies guide model and training configurations under given compute budget [3, 50]. Extending this framework to jointly account for branch count, branch depth, and hidden dimensions could identify how best to allocate parameters within that budget. Incorporating inference cost would further guide configurations that balance modeling quality and serving efficiency. MBT + YOCO + Cross-Layer Attention. YOCO enables aggressive cache reduction and early-exit prefill [49], while Cross-Layer Attention shares KV across neighboring layers [48]. Recent work such as HySparse2 combines selective sharing across layers with sparse attention [51]. Combining these approaches with MBT 14 Multi-Branch Transformer would enable joint design of KV sharing across branches and layers, potentially improving the trade-off between modeling quality, prefill efficiency, and decoding speed. MBTs for Multimodality. Multimodal Transformers such as MM-DiT already use distinct parameters for different modalities [52]. MBTs could extend this idea to branches that serve as text, image, or audio backbones, with widths, depths, and block types tailored to each modality. Studying where these branches should interact and fuse could improve the balance between modality specialization and cross-modal information exchange. Multi-Branch Transformer
